slides.text: Old Ezra had operated his pawnshop on 4th Street for forty years and thought he had appraised every tragedy human desperation could produce. That changed when a pale woman in a yellow raincoat sold him a fireproof lockbox with no key for fifty dollars and sprinted into the blinding rain without taking her receipt. Ezra took a heavy drill to the brass tumbler. Inside lay no jewelry or bearer bonds—only an unspooled microcassette labeled in fresh black ink: 'Listen at 11:42 PM.'

At 11:41 PM, sitting alone beneath the buzzing neon sign of his shop with a cup of black coffee, Ezra loaded the tape into an old Dictaphone and pressed play. Through heavy tape hiss, a voice began speaking. Ezra’s coffee mug slipped from his hand, shattering across the counter. The voice on the recording was unmistakably his own—raspy, breathless, speaking in a frantic cadence he had never used: 'Ezra, if you're hearing this, he’s already inside the crawlspace. Don't look at the cellar trapdoor.'

Ezra stood frozen in terror. The voice on the tape continued, narrating his exact movements in real time: 'You just dropped your mug. You're reaching for the revolver under the register. Don't. It's empty. He took the bullets an hour ago.' Ezra whipped open the drawer; the six brass cartridges were gone. Behind him, from the dark corridor leading to the cellar stairs, the floorboard gave a slow, deliberate creak. And from the darkness, a voice whispered: 'Tape's almost over, Ezra.'
